title: Podcast with Harry Kumar, Co-founder, Director & CCO of Moth Quantum - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Moth Quantum co-founder Harry Kumar explains Quantum Backrooms, a browser game whose maze is generated on real quantum hardware with no claimed speedup, and Atlas, a hardware-agnostic platform letting non-experts build quantum music, image and game tools. He argues quantum today resembles generative AI in 2016, when creative engagement preceded commercial value.

insights.claim: Quantum Backrooms maps each map tile to a qubit and decides whether a wall exists between tiles from the correlation between the two qubits, so players effectively explore the quantum processor as it evolves toward a creatively chosen end state.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Shows a concrete non-chemistry use of QPU dynamics; watch whether such mechanics generate hardware usage.
insights.quote: each tile is essentially a qubit
insights.locator: Every tile is a qubit

insights.claim: The game grew from a researcher's paper on quantum imaginary time evolution, reappropriating an algorithm normally used to optimize toward a ground energy state in quantum chemistry for building game levels.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Illustrates how research algorithms get repurposed into demos that market the platform.
insights.locator: Every tile is a qubit

insights.claim: Moth timed the game launch with the Backrooms film release, and the Backrooms theme was chosen partly by luck when the CTO saw that shifting walls resemble superposition.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Cultural-timing marketing is a low-cost way for a quantum startup to gain attention.
insights.locator: Why Moth built a Backrooms game

insights.claim: At a Gamescom booth, visitors from kids to quantum-industry people set their own end state and generated personal Quantum Backrooms levels on IBM Fez or IBM Miami hardware.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Evidence of real-hardware consumer-facing usage via IBM devices.
insights.locator: No quantum advantage, and why that is the point

insights.claim: Moth explicitly refuses to claim any quantum advantage or performance gain for Quantum Backrooms over a classically built game, because current hardware cannot deliver speedups or solve intractable problems.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Rare candor from a quantum company; useful contrast with hype-driven claims.
insights.quote: Or that backrooms presents any kind of performance upgrade to a classically developed game.
insights.locator: No quantum advantage, and why that is the point

insights.claim: Quantum random number generation output cannot be told apart by eye from classical randomness, so creative uses of quantum today are valued for engagement rather than measurable difference.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Limits near-term commercial claims for QRNG-based creative tools.
insights.locator: Can you hear quantum randomness?

insights.claim: Classical computers can only produce pseudo-randomness, whereas a quantum computer has real randomness built in because it computes with nature, a framing Kumar ties to Feynman's 1980s lecture.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: The 'true randomness' pitch is the simplest quantum differentiator for consumer and creative products.
insights.locator: Pseudo-randomness and computing with nature

insights.claim: Moth is not focused on building games; its main product is Atlas, a platform used to make Quantum Backrooms that lets anyone build quantum games, music tools or image tools at an abstracted level, and it began releasing to an alpha user group that week.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Positions Moth as picks-and-shovels tooling rather than a content studio.
insights.locator: Atlas: a platform, not a games studio

insights.claim: Moth compares Atlas to Epic Games shipping Unreal Engine alongside Fortnite, with generalized engines such as quantum graph that can be applied to music, images, video or even DNA sequences.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Engine-style licensing could create platform lock-in if adoption materializes.
insights.locator: Who is quantum creativity for?

insights.claim: Atlas offers a no-code image engine where a user drops in a JPEG or PNG, moves sliders and runs it on an emulator or real quantum hardware, and the platform aims to be as hardware agnostic as possible.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Hardware-agnostic middleware could shift demand toward whichever QPUs Atlas supports.
insights.locator: Who is quantum creativity for?

insights.claim: Moth's entanglement shader computes light coefficients to render physically accurate iridescence in Blender and will be offered on Atlas as a core engine, with one suggestion being to repurpose it as a reverb plugin.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Shows the cross-domain reuse Moth bets on.
insights.locator: From an entanglement shader to a reverb plugin

insights.claim: In the week before the interview, roughly six or seven new quantum music tools were created by alpha users that call the Atlas API each time they run, on emulation or real hardware.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Early traction indicator to track via API call counts and user growth.
insights.locator: Which modality makes the best beats?

insights.claim: Atlas is in alpha; users can run on an emulator with their own key, heavy users get free compute credits, and Moth plans an open call for creative projects and an online hackathon the following week.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Community-building spend signals a user-acquisition-first strategy.
insights.locator: Where to try Atlas

insights.claim: Kumar argues quantum computing is sometimes described as a solution looking for a problem, and that the full space of applications will only be unlocked once a broader set of people than the narrow chemistry, cryptography and pharma demographic engages with it.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Frames consumer experimentation as an application-discovery channel.
insights.quote: a solution looking for a problem
insights.locator: Who is quantum creativity for?

insights.claim: Quantum today is analogous to AI in 2016: early outputs like Deep Dream and Terence Broad's Blade Runner Auto Encoded were not commercially useful yet attracted creatives, and by 2020-21 DALL-E drew a million waitlist sign-ups despite janky images.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: If the analogy holds, creative adoption precedes commercial value; useful as a lens for quantum software startups.
insights.locator: Can you hear quantum randomness?

insights.claim: Kumar calls creative engagement on real quantum hardware one of the only things one can do with quantum today where someone finds value, and sees it as the step before real commercial value.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Suggests near-term quantum revenue from novelty rather than advantage.
insights.locator: Can you hear quantum randomness?

insights.claim: Kumar expects timelines to reach a point within a few years where quantum computers do things that cannot be simulated classically.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Aligns with industry timelines but is stated without specifics.
insights.locator: Who is quantum creativity for?

insights.claim: Moth predicts it will have one of the most engaged active user bases in quantum and says running varied circuits across multiple modalities produces data valuable to hardware partners.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Hardware vendors may value Moth as a source of diverse workloads and user acquisition.
insights.locator: How the quantum industry sees Moth

insights.claim: Quantum Backrooms acted as an unintended benchmark: across devices from several hardware providers, Moth's team could identify the hardware used from the levels it produced.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Indicates device-specific noise signatures are visible in creative outputs.
insights.locator: How the quantum industry sees Moth

insights.claim: Moth declined to name which qubit modality it uses or prefers for music, saying its intuition is not valuable and it wants users to test that.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: No modality preference signal can be taken from Moth.
insights.locator: Which modality makes the best beats?

themes.theme: AI and the death of the first draft

insights.claim: Kumar tries not to let AI replace his thinking, arguing the first draft holds much of the thinking and outsourcing it or the original idea makes the mind less capable of creativity and challenging ideas.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: A creator-side argument against delegating ideation to AI.
insights.locator: The handover question: AI and the first draft

insights.claim: Kumar uses AI for administrative work such as expense receipts and calls Claude Code the most significant app since Google search for letting non-coders build software, while acknowledging bloated code outputs.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Adds anecdotal evidence of vibe-coding adoption among non-developers.
insights.quote: impossible to admit that Claude Code in particular for coding things is an extraordinary development in technology
insights.locator: The handover question: AI and the first draft

insights.claim: Kumar poses whether one could enjoy media generated solely by an autonomous system, which he calls 'auto culture'.
insights.speaker: Harry Kumar
insights.so_what: Open question on demand for fully autonomous AI-generated media.
insights.locator: The handover question: AI and the first draft
